paragraphs.heading: What a state of matter is
paragraphs.text: A state of matter, also called a phase of matter, is one of the separate forms that matter can take. Four of them turn up in ordinary life: solid, liquid, gas and plasma. What sets them apart is how their tiny parts, such as atoms, molecules, ions and electrons, are laid out and how they behave as a group.

paragraphs.heading: Solids
paragraphs.text: In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and stay in fixed spots. The pull between them is so strong that they cannot wander off, only vibrate where they are. That is why a solid keeps a set shape and a set volume, and changes shape only when an outside force breaks or cuts it. In crystalline solids the particles sit in a regular, repeating pattern, and one substance can have more than one such pattern. Iron, for example, switches from one cubic arrangement to another at 912 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Liquids
paragraphs.text: In a liquid, the particles stay close but can slide past each other. The forces between them still matter, yet the particles have enough energy to move around, so the structure is mobile. A liquid therefore takes the shape of whatever holds it while keeping a nearly constant volume, and it is very hard to squeeze. A liquid usually takes up more room than the same substance as a solid, and water, H₂O, is the best known exception.

paragraphs.heading: Gases and plasma
paragraphs.text: Gas particles sit far from one another and roam freely. They carry so much energy of motion that the forces between them have little effect, and the gap between neighbours is much larger than the particles themselves. A gas is a fluid that can be squeezed into less space. It has no set shape or volume, and spreads out to fill its whole container. Plasma is like a gas, but it also holds charged particles, ions and free electrons, that move on their own and respond to electric and magnetic fields.

paragraphs.heading: Changing state
paragraphs.text: Matter can move from one state to another. Melting turns a solid into a liquid, and freezing does the reverse. A solid can also skip the liquid stage and become a gas directly, which is called sublimation, while the jump back from gas to solid is called deposition. Heating a liquid to its boiling point, or lowering the pressure on it, turns it into a gas. A gas usually becomes a plasma either through a huge voltage between two points or through extremely high temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the classic four
paragraphs.text: Many more states exist beyond these four. Some sit in between: liquid crystals behave partly like solids and partly like liquids. Magnetic states depend not on where the atoms are but on how their built-in magnetic moments, called spins, line up. Others appear only in extreme conditions, such as Bose–Einstein condensates in extreme cold, or quark–gluon plasma at extremely high energy.

paragraphs.heading: Phases within a state
paragraphs.text: The word phase is sometimes used to mean a state of matter, but one substance can form several phases while staying in the same state. Ice is solid water, yet it has fifteen known crystal structures that form at different temperatures and pressures. The line between liquid and gas can blur too. Above its critical temperature and critical pressure, a gas becomes a supercritical fluid, in which liquid and gas can no longer be told apart. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used to remove caffeine when making decaffeinated coffee.
